entry.summary: A visa is needed, arranged through the Tourism Council of Bhutan, with the Sustainable Development Fee.
entry.other: Some areas need extra permits, arranged through your guide. Bhutan doesn't recognise de facto or same-sex relationships for dependent visas.

money-and-cost.cash_card_notes: The official currency is the Bhutanese Ngultrum (BTN). The Indian Rupee (INR) is also legal tender, but larger banknotes may not be accepted. ATMs are common in towns. EFTPOS is available nationwide, including at most hotels. Credit cards aren't widely accepted, but you can use them at major hotels.

consular.notes: Australia doesn't have an embassy or consulate in Bhutan. For consular assistance, contact the Australian High Commission in New Delhi, India.

laws.rule: Penalties for drug offences are severe and include long jail terms and heavy fines. Penalties apply for using marijuana.
laws.heading: Drugs

laws.rule: The amendment of the Tobacco Control Act of Bhutan 2010 legalizes the import, sale and buying of tobacco and tobacco products in the country.
laws.heading: Other laws

laws.rule: Same-sex activity has been decriminalised. There's no legal recognition of same-sex relationships. Consider limiting public displays of affection.
laws.heading: LGBTQIA+ travellers

laws.rule: You may need to have medical documents authenticated by DFAT before you leave.
laws.heading: Medications

laws.rule: Travellers rarely drive in Bhutan. Most use organised tours and local drivers.
laws.heading: Driving permit

culture-and-protocol.dress_and_conduct: Bhutan has conservative standards of dress and behaviour. Take care not to offend. If you visit temples or other religious institutions, dress modestly and respectfully. Long pants are most appropriate for men. Long skirts are most appropriate for women.
